summary: Trent, a Tata Group company, runs Westside and Zudio clothing stores that sell clothes, shoes and beauty products under its own labels. It also runs Star supermarkets with a partner and owns part of Zara’s Indian stores.
description: Trent designs clothes, footwear, beauty products and home items, has suppliers make them, and sells them in its own shops and online. Westside stores, mostly 20,000 to 30,000 square feet, sell mid-priced fashion and home goods. Zudio stores, around 10,000 to 12,000 square feet, sell clothes and beauty products at low prices. At 30 September 2026 it ran 311 Westside, 999 Zudio and 32 other fashion stores in 339 cities; three of those cities are in the United Arab Emirates. Star supermarkets sell groceries, fresh food and daily needs.
money: Trent earns money by selling goods to shoppers in its stores and online. The price on the tag, minus GST, is its revenue. It spends on buying the clothes and other goods from suppliers, store rent, staff, warehouses and moving stock to stores, and on opening new stores. Clothes that do not sell must be marked down or written off. The shopper’s payment is revenue, not profit.
customers: Shoppers pay at the till or online for the clothes, shoes, cosmetics and home items they take home. Westside also sells through Westside.com, Tata Cliq and Tata Neu. Star’s shoppers buy groceries and fresh produce. Booker Wholesale sells in bulk to kirana stores (small neighbourhood shops), traders, hotels, restaurants and caterers.
drivers: How many new stores open and how quickly they fill up, how much each existing store sells compared with a year earlier, and whether prices stay steady while the cost of buying goods and renting stores rises.

groups.title: Westside
groups.examples: Shirts, dresses, children’s clothes, shoes, perfume, bedsheets and home décor under Westside’s own labels.
groups.explanation: Mid-priced fashion and home goods in large stores and online. Westside designs the products in-house, so shoppers find items they cannot buy elsewhere.

groups.title: Zudio
groups.examples: Low-priced T-shirts, jeans, kurtas, children’s wear, footwear and cosmetics.
groups.explanation: Value fashion in smaller stores. Trent says Zudio’s products are designed in-house and priced very sharply. Most new Zudio stores are opening in smaller cities.

groups.title: Newer fashion labels
groups.examples: Utsa for Indian-style women’s wear, Samoh for wedding and occasion wear, and Burnt Toast for young shoppers.
groups.explanation: Smaller brands Trent is still building. It says newer brands such as Burnt Toast and Samoh are at varying stages of development.

groups.title: Star supermarkets
groups.examples: Vegetables, fruit, dairy, staples such as rice and dal, and packaged goods, many under Star’s own brands.
groups.explanation: Grocery stores run mainly by a company Trent owns half of with Tesco of the UK. Star had 87 stores in 13 cities at 30 September 2026.

groups.title: Booker Wholesale and partner stores
groups.examples: Bulk staples, snacks, soap and soft drinks for small shops; Zara and Massimo Dutti stores in India.
groups.explanation: Booker is a cash-and-carry wholesaler: business customers come, pay and take goods away. Trent also owns 20% of the companies running Zara and Massimo Dutti stores in India.

basics.title: What is an own brand?
basics.text: A label that the shop itself owns. Trent designs the product and pays a supplier to make it, then sells it only in its stores. It decides the price and keeps the gap between the factory cost and the shelf price, but it also takes the risk if the stock does not sell.

basics.title: What is like-for-like growth?
basics.text: Sales growth counted only from stores that have been open for more than 18 months. It shows whether existing stores are selling more, separate from growth that comes from opening new stores.

basics.title: Why are only some Star sales in Trent’s revenue?
basics.text: Most Star stores are run by Trent Hypermarket, a company Trent owns jointly with Tesco. For a jointly owned company, accounting rules let Trent add only its share of profit or loss, not its sales. Star stores run by Fiora Hypermarket, a company inside the Trent group, are counted in full.

steps.title: Design the range
steps.text: Trent’s teams decide what to sell each season and design it under their own labels.

steps.title: Have it made and stored
steps.text: Suppliers, mostly in India, make the goods. Trent pays them, receives the stock in its warehouses and sends it to stores. It owns the stock until a shopper buys it.

steps.title: Sell in the store or online
steps.text: A shopper pays at the till or online and takes the item home. Trent prefers to run its stores itself and uses franchising only selectively.

steps.title: Clear what did not sell
steps.text: Unsold items are marked down in end-of-season sales or written down in value. This reduces profit even though the clothes were already paid for.

steps.title: Pay rent and open more stores
steps.text: From what remains, Trent pays rent, staff and transport, and invests in new stores and warehouses. Revenue (the shopper’s payment, without GST), profit (what is left after all costs) and cash in the bank are different things.

specifics.title: It owns the brands and runs the stores
specifics.text: Trent sells mostly its own labels through stores it operates and keeps ownership of the stock until it is sold. It controls the price and design, but it also carries the cost of stock that does not sell.

specifics.title: Growth comes mainly from new stores
specifics.text: Trent says it has opened around 250 stores a year in recent years, many in smaller cities. It says newer markets take two to three years to become fully relevant, so new stores sell less at first.

specifics.title: Steady prices instead of discounts
specifics.text: Trent says it does not use price as a short-term lever to manage demand. When costs rise, it tries to absorb them through sourcing and efficiency rather than raising tag prices.

specifics.title: Some rent moves with sales
specifics.text: Trent’s January to March 2026 presentation says some store rents and fees paid to property partners rise and fall with store sales, so part of the rent bill shrinks in a weak month.

watch: Are existing stores still selling more each year?
If only new stores add sales, growth stops when store openings slow.
Read the like-for-like growth line in each quarterly investor presentation and compare it with total revenue growth.
Are new stores in smaller cities paying off?
Trent says newer markets take longer to mature, and each new store costs money to fit out and stock.
Follow store counts, cities and retail area in each presentation, and compare revenue per square foot over several years.
Is rising cost of goods squeezing profit?
Trent keeps prices steady, so higher fabric and supplier costs come out of its margin.
Compare operating profit as a share of revenue each quarter and read the market context slides for comments on inflation.
Star needs investment in stores, and its profit or loss reaches Trent only as a share.
Find the share of profit or loss from joint ventures in the consolidated results, and Star’s revenue and own-brand share in each presentation.
How much stock is sitting unsold?
Unsold clothes tie up cash and may later be marked down.
Compare inventory on the balance sheet with revenue in each annual report, and read the notes on inventory written down for slow-moving stock.
risks: Clothes and cosmetics are easy to put off buying. Trent said in early 2026 that consumers were spending with caution.
Trent says inflation across its costs remains elevated. Because it keeps its prices steady, higher costs reduce what it earns on each item.
Trent says competition in Indian fashion retail has been high for several years. Rivals with lower prices or more stores can take shoppers.
Many new stores are in smaller cities that Trent says take longer to mature, so they may earn less for some years while still paying rent and staff.
Trent describes Star’s competitive landscape as evolving. Star needs investment in new stores before it earns a steady profit.
context: July to September 2026: the 1,000th Zudio store

On 29 October 2026 Trent said it opened its 1,000th Zudio store during the quarter. At 30 September 2026 it ran 311 Westside stores against 261 a year earlier, and 999 Zudio stores against 806. In the quarter it opened 10 Westside and 19 Zudio stores. Trent says the full year is more representative than one quarter, because store openings are uneven.

financialNotes.title: Standalone, consolidated and Star
financialNotes.text: Trent reports standalone results (Westside, Zudio and other fashion) and consolidated results. Consolidated revenue does not include the sales of Star stores run by the Tesco joint venture, only Trent’s share of their profit or loss. Trent’s own operating profit measures leave out lease accounting effects, so compare them with reported profit. Verified full-year figures for this profile have not yet been added, so the financial table below is marked as awaiting verification.

stepsTitle: From a design table to a shopping bag.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: Trent designs its own clothes and beauty products, has suppliers make them, and sells them in Westside and Zudio stores. It also runs grocery stores with a partner.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Shoppers pay at the till or online. Small shops and restaurants pay Booker Wholesale for goods bought in bulk.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: From selling goods. Because the brands are its own, it does not share the shelf price with a separate brand owner.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Buying stock from suppliers, store rent, staff, warehouses and transport, and the cost of opening hundreds of new stores each year.

helps.title: Own brands sold directly
helps.text: Trent designs its products and sells them directly to shoppers. It says this lets it set its own value for money and stand apart from rivals, instead of selling the same brands as every other shop.

helps.title: Clusters of stores in the same area
helps.text: Trent adds stores close to each other in chosen areas. It says greater density, together with better stores, is lifting sales and profit for each cluster.

helps.title: Prices shoppers can rely on
helps.text: Trent keeps its prices broadly stable across categories and seasons. It says a steady price structure and steady margins build trust in its brands over time.

hurts.title: Clothes are easy to put off buying
hurts.text: Clothes and cosmetics are purchases people can put off when money is tight. Trent said in early 2026 that shoppers were cutting back on such spending.

hurts.title: Rising costs with steady prices
hurts.text: Because Trent keeps its prices steady, higher costs for fabric, suppliers and transport come out of what it earns on each item until savings are found elsewhere.

hurts.title: Heavy competition
hurts.text: Trent says competition in Indian fashion retail has been high for several years. Rivals with lower prices or more stores can take shoppers.

hurts.title: New towns take years to pay back
hurts.text: Many new stores are in smaller cities that Trent says take two to three years to mature. Meanwhile they still pay rent, staff and fit-out costs.
